answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: Over ten years, mostly at Kestrel Remit, I've owned transaction boundaries across three different services -- the one that still sticks with me is our cross-border transfer engine, handling something like 40,000 remittances a day at peak, mostly USD-to-PHP and USD-to-MXN corridors. Early on, the boundary wrapped the full transfer: debit the sender, call the FX-rate lock, call the payout-partner API, all in one transaction. Under partner-API latency spikes -- sometimes 8-10 seconds during their maintenance windows -- that held row locks on the sender's balance long enough to cause contention across unrelated transfers to the same corridor. I split it into three phases: debit-and-hold commits first, FX lock happens as its own step, and payout dispatch happens last, each with its own compensating reversal path. The first version of the FX-lock step had a gap -- if the lock expired before payout dispatch ran, we'd occasionally lock a rate twice for the same transfer under retry, which we only found after a customer complained about being charged two different rates for one transfer. That taught me to make every phase explicitly idempotent against retry, not just the whole transaction.
answers.says: Names a concrete transaction-boundary problem in a production Java service they were responsible for (e.g., lock contention on a long transaction, an external API call left inside a transaction, inconsistency from an isolation level), describes where they moved the boundary and the grounds for that decision (measurements, a real incident, data-consistency requirements), and covers the outcome or the fix for a failure, with numbers and time frames. Beyond just ‘we did it as a team,’ their own judgment and hands-on work are clear, and they can explain a design failure in their own words.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: About four years ago, our transfer-dispatch service started getting OOMKilled on Kubernetes roughly four to five times a week during evening peak -- 6pm to 9pm Pacific, when both US and Latin American traffic overlap. GC logs showed G1 doing full collections every couple of minutes under load; heap was 4GB against a workload generating large temporary objects for every FX-rate lookup. I redesigned the rate-lookup path to reuse a shared, immutable snapshot object instead of allocating a fresh one per request, bumped heap to 8GB, and separately found our connection pool capped at 20 against a workload that needed closer to 60 during peak. p99 on transfer dispatch went from about 3.8 seconds to under 500ms, and OOMKills dropped to zero over the following six weeks. I tried horizontal scaling first, adding three more pods -- it helped throughput a little but didn't touch the pause-time problem, since each pod still hit the same per-object allocation issue.
answers.says: Names a concrete operational problem in a Java service they operated (e.g., latency degradation from GC pauses, connection pool exhaustion, an OOM on Kubernetes), and describes the measurement tools used, the numbers obtained, the changes tried, the results (with figures), and, if the first fix missed, the failure and the retry. Can explain the triage process in their own words, with grounds for the decisions rather than a list of tool names.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I don't have production Rust experience, but I've been seriously working toward it for the last several months -- I finished the official book, built a small command-line tool that parses our FX-rate feed format as practice, and I'm now reading through the tokio documentation since our transfer-dispatch service is heavily async. My realistic estimate is another two to three months of side projects before I'd trust myself on anything production-facing, and I'd want to pair with someone who has shipped Rust before on the first real piece. On migration, given ten years of watching what happens when a team gets excited and rewrites too much at once, I'd want to pick the narrowest, most measurable piece -- probably the FX-rate lock service, since it's CPU-bound and has a clean boundary -- and run it alongside the Java version in shadow for at least a full settlement cycle before trusting it.
answers.says: If they have production Rust experience, they describe which part of production it was (e.g., why latency became an issue, how they cut the boundary with Java, the measurement results), with numbers and time frames, and can describe failures too. If they lack production experience, they explain the concrete differences from Java in ownership, lifetimes, and async runtimes in their own words, and describe a realistic learning plan (what they have already written, read, or been studying). In addition, they state a view that fits our approach — deciding a boundary and migrating while measuring, rather than a full rewrite — together with their own grounds for it.

answers.text: Tell me about a concrete incident where the numbers didn't match in settlement or reconciliation. What was off, by how much, how did you notice, what was the cause, and how did you correct it? Please also cover how you handled data after it was finalized.
answers.answer: About two years ago, our monthly reconciliation against one partner's settlement report showed a mismatch of around $4,200 on a total settlement volume in the tens of millions -- small relative to volume, but it shouldn't have been there. I traced it to a batch of transfers that had been refunded by the partner after our reconciliation window closed for that month but before the partner's own report cutoff, a timing mismatch between when we considered a period closed and when they did. It affected about 60 transfers across that one partner relationship. We corrected it with new adjusting entries for each affected transfer rather than editing the original closed records, and moved our reconciliation window to run three days later in the month to give late refunds time to settle before we closed the books. My first theory was a currency-conversion rounding issue, which I ruled out once the mismatch amount didn't scale with transfer volume the way a rounding error would.
answers.says: Names a concrete mismatch they chased down themselves (the amount, the count, when they noticed), and describes the triage approach, the cause, the fix (e.g., correcting it with a new record rather than an overwrite once it was finalized), and the prevention of recurrence, with numbers and time frames. Can also describe a point where their initial read was wrong.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: Early in my time at Kestrel, I shipped a config change that silently disabled retry on a non-critical notification queue -- not the transfer path itself, but customer-facing SMS confirmations. I noticed it myself the next day when delivery-rate metrics looked off, and told my manager within the hour, before any customer had complained. I've been on the transfer-platform on-call rotation for about eight years now, roughly one week in five, and I still take escalations from our support team when a customer disputes a transfer status. I've mentored six or seven engineers over the years, several of whom are now senior themselves, mostly around how to read our reconciliation reports and think about failure modes in payment systems.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: In Rust code you've actually written — production or a personal project, either is fine — tell me a spot where you got stuck on ownership, lifetimes, or async, and how you resolved it. If you haven't written any yet, just say so.
answers.answer: I've only written the small CLI tool I mentioned -- a parser for our FX-rate feed format, built as a personal exercise, not production. The place I actually got stuck was trying to hold a reference to a parsed rate record across an async boundary while also mutating a shared cache of recent rates; the borrow checker wouldn't let me do both at once. I ended up restructuring it so the parsing step returns owned data instead of borrowed references, and the cache update happens as a separate step after, rather than trying to do both inside one async block. It's a small thing, but it's the first time ownership actually clicked for me instead of just reading about it.
answers.says: Names concretely what failed to compile in their own code (e.g., a borrow conflict, a lifetime annotation, a Send/Sync constraint, a tokio runtime boundary), how they fixed it, and how they came to understand the fix, in their own words. If it was production work, which part of production it was comes out concretely; if personal, what they built comes out concretely.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: If I were moving part of our transfer ledger write path to Rust, I'd start with the FX-rate lock step I mentioned -- narrow, stateless between calls, no direct database ownership needed since it just returns a locked rate and an expiry. I'd keep the boundary as an internal gRPC call from the Java dispatch service, with the Rust service owning nothing but the lock logic itself, and the actual ledger write staying in Java. Before and after, I'd measure lock-acquisition latency, memory per instance, and -- critically for this specific piece -- the rate of double-locks under retry, since that's the exact failure mode I described earlier. I'd want at least a full settlement cycle of shadow traffic, comparing Rust's decisions against the Java path's decisions on the same requests, before cutting over anything live.
answers.says: Concretely describes how to choose a migration target (measuring hot paths, starting with lower-risk parts), how to place the boundary (the shape of the interface, how to keep data consistent, coexisting with Java), and what metrics to watch before and after migration (latency, memory, correctness reconciliation), together with their own grounds for those decisions. If they've carved out a boundary before, they include the numbers, failures, and how they built agreement with the team. Fits our ‘decide the boundary before you rewrite’ approach, and can also describe how they resisted the temptation to do a full rewrite.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: At Kestrel Remit, every transfer request carries an idempotency key generated client-side, stored in Postgres with a unique constraint, and every retry from our own dispatch logic reuses that same key rather than generating a new one. About three years ago, a partner-API integration for a new corridor had a bug where their webhook confirming payout could fire twice for the same transfer under certain network conditions -- over about five weeks we found 340 transfers out of roughly 1.4 million processed in that window where we'd logged two confirmation events, though the unique constraint on our payout-confirmation table meant zero duplicate payouts actually went out. What it did expose was that our alerting only fired on payment attempts, not confirmation duplicates, so we were blind to it for those five weeks. We added a separate alert on duplicate confirmation events and fixed the partner-side webhook handling to dedupe by their event ID before processing.
answers.says: Names the concrete mechanism they implemented and operated (idempotency-key design, store choice, duplicate-delivery detection, reconciliation mechanism), why they chose that design, and the process of noticing and recovering when an incident or duplication actually occurred, with numbers (scale, count, time taken) and time frames. If it was an experience of resolving a consistency mismatch, they can also describe the root-cause triage and the grounds for correcting it with a new journal entry or record rather than an overwrite.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: During the duplicate-confirmation incident, I wanted to skip our second-reviewer requirement to ship the dedupe fix faster, since I was confident in the change. I didn't -- I asked another senior engineer for a focused twenty-minute review instead of our usual next-day cycle, explained why it was urgent, and they caught that my dedupe key didn't account for one of the partner's older event formats still in use for legacy corridors. Outside a live incident like that, I've never skipped review or the deploy procedure in ten years, and on a system moving people's remittances to family members abroad, I don't think any amount of speed is worth getting that wrong.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
